from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: Scaling Laws", [
            "Scaling determines how an object fills space.",
            "Line segments scale with the power of one.",
            "Squares scale with the power of two."
        ])
        
        # Colors
        c1 = "#00FFFF" # Cyan
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Scaling determines how an object fills space.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(c1)
        line = Line(LEFT, RIGHT, color=c1)
        self.place_at_grid(line, "C2")
        self.play(Create(line))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Line segments scale with the power of one.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(c1)
        # Scale segment by factor 2, revealing 2 segments total.
        line_scaled = VGroup(
            Line(LEFT*0.5, ORIGIN, color=c1),
            Line(ORIGIN, RIGHT*0.5, color=c1)
        ).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0)
        self.place_at_grid(line_scaled, "C4")
        self.play(Transform(line, line_scaled))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Squares scale with the power of two.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(c1)
        # Demonstrate 2^1 copies when scaling by factor 2.
        # Actually for 2D square divided into 2x2 squares (factor 2, N=4)
        square = Square(side_length=1.5, color=c1, fill_opacity=0.3)
        self.place_at_grid(square, "E3")
        self.play(Create(square))
        
        four_squares = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.75, color=c1, fill_opacity=0.5) for _ in range(4)])
        four_squares.arrange_in_grid(2, 2, buff=0)
        self.place_at_grid(four_squares, "E5")
        
        self.play(Transform(square, four_squares))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Fractal dimension bridges the gap between integers.", 
                         "We use logarithms to measure scaling behavior.", 
                         "The formula quantifies space-filling capacity.", 
                         "Koch snowflakes demonstrate this fractional dimension.", 
                         "Dimension is a measure of roughness."]
        self.setup_layout("Defining the Fractal Dimension (Hausdorff)", lecture_lines)
        
        # Elements
        formula = MathTex(r"D = \frac{\log(N)}{\log(1/r)}", font_size=42, color=GOLD)
        n_label = MathTex("N", color=BLUE).next_to(formula, UP, buff=0.5)
        r_label = MathTex("r", color=RED).next_to(formula, DOWN, buff=0.5)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(GOLD)
        self.play(Write(formula))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(BLUE)
        self.play(FadeIn(n_label))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(RED)
        self.play(FadeIn(r_label))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[3].set_color(GREEN)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, 'D3')
        self.play(formula.animate.scale(1.2))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color(PURPLE)
        self.play(Indicate(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        lecture_lines = ["Iteration increases the object's perceived density.",

                         "Recursive patterns trap area within limited boundaries.",

        self.place_at_grid(sierpinski_2, "C3", scale_factor=1.5)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Nature utilizes fractals for efficient surface area.",
            "Bronchial trees maximize gas exchange through complexity.",
            "Dimension helps diagnose health and monitor systems."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application: Nature's Geometry", lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors
        color1 = "#4CAF50" # Nature green
        color2 = "#2196F3" # Bronchial blue
        color3 = "#FF9800" # Health orange

        # Assets (Simulated with geometric shapes as requested/implied)
        # 1. Nature fractal representation
        nature_obj = VGroup(
            *[Triangle().scale(0.5).set_color(color1) for _ in range(5)]
        ).arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=3)
        
        # 2. Bronchial tree concept
        tree_obj = VGroup(
            Line(ORIGIN, UP*1),
            Line(UP*1, UP*1.5 + RIGHT*0.5),
            Line(UP*1, UP*1.5 + LEFT*0.5)
        ).set_color(color2).set_stroke(width=4)

        # 3. Fractal dimension label
        dim_label = MathTex(r"D \approx 2.7", color=color3).scale(1.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(color1)
        self.place_in_area(nature_obj, 'A1', 'C6', scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(FadeIn(nature_obj))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(color2)
        self.play(FadeOut(nature_obj))
        self.place_at_grid(tree_obj, 'C3', scale_factor=1.5)
        self.play(Create(tree_obj))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(color3)
        self.place_at_grid(dim_label, 'D3', scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(dim_label))
        self.wait(1)

sections.title: The Failure of Traditional Dimensions
sections.content: Introduce topological dimension (0D point, 1D line, 2D plane). Pose the paradox: How do we measure the 'roughness' of objects like a coastline or a lung that fill space more than a line but less than a plane?
sections.example: Visual transition from a smooth circle to a jagged, self-similar Koch Snowflake.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Scaling Laws
sections.content: Define the relationship between length (L), scale factor (r), and number of pieces (N). Explain that in 1D, N=1/r; in 2D, N=1/r². This sets the stage for the power-law exponent.
sections.example: A 1D line segment cut into 3 pieces (r=1/3, N=3); a 2D square divided into 3x3 smaller squares (r=1/3, N=9).

sections.title: Defining the Fractal Dimension (Hausdorff)
sections.content: Derive the formula: D = log(N) / log(1/r). Explain that if N is not an integer power of 1/r, D becomes a non-integer, quantifying the 'space-filling' capacity.
sections.example: Applying the formula to the Koch Snowflake (N=4, r=1/3), resulting in D ≈ 1.26.

sections.title: Visualizing Complexity
sections.content: Animate the dimension growth: show how increasing the iterations of a fractal makes the object increasingly dense, effectively 'trapping' more space.
sections.example: The Sierpinski Triangle: Starting with a triangle (2D), remove the middle, leaving 3 parts with half the side length, resulting in D = log(3)/log(2) ≈ 1.58.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Nature's Geometry
sections.content: Conclude by showing how fractal dimensions allow engineers and biologists to quantify complexity in natural systems that standard geometry fails to describe.
sections.example: Comparing the fractal dimension of a healthy human bronchial tree (highly efficient gas exchange) versus a diseased one (lower fractal dimension/loss of complexity).
